newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan says Castro agrees to take in Peru rebels.
newsitem.headline: Japan says Castro agrees to take in Peru rebels.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said on Thursday that Cuban President Fidel Castro had formally agreed to take in rebels holding hostages in Peru if it would help end the crisis.
Hashimoto was speaking after a Japanese envoy delivered a personal appeal to Castro in Havana from the prime minister asking Cuba to give the rebels asylum on humanitarian grounds.
"I hope this will accelerate moves to seek an early solution," Hashimoto told reporters.

Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas took over the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima on December 17 during a diplomatic reception attended by hundreds of guests and are still holding 72 hostages.
They are demanding the release of jailed comrades.
Japanese government sources in Tokyo said Castro told the envoy, Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura, that Cuba agreed to the asylum request purely as a humanitarian gesture.
"Our acceptance on this issue is from a humanitarian point of view. Cuba is not a country to take in terrorism," the sources quoted Castro as saying.
Komura arrived in Havana after a two-day visit to Lima as part of Hashimoto's efforts to speed up a solution of the hostage drama.
Castro also told Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori in Havana earlier this month that Cuba was willing to grant asylum to the hostage-takers.
The Cuban leader, calling such an offer a "moral duty," said at the time that all parties involved, including the rebels, would have to agree formally to such a move.
Following Fujimori's trip to Havana, the rebels told reporters they wanted to stay in Peru but said they reserved comment on the possibility of asylum in Cuba.

Komura was to travel Thursday afternoon to the Dominican Republic, which like Cuba has offered asylum for some of the MRTA members. Despite the diplomatic moves, the MRTA has given no indication it will accept asylum or end its siege with anything less than the release of its jailed members.
